title: ConfigMaps, Secrets & Ingress
description: Manage configuration and sensitive data, and route external traffic using Ingress controllers.

data.text: The **twelve-factor app** says configuration should be separated from code. In Kubernetes, a **ConfigMap** is the way to store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs. You can inject these values into Pods as environment variables, command-line arguments, or configuration files.

data.title: Creating a ConfigMap
data.content: Define a ConfigMap with application configuration values.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
 data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "debug"
  API_URL: "https://api.example.com"
  TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "30"

data.title: Using a ConfigMap in a Pod
data.content: Inject ConfigMap values as environment variables and mount as a config file.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:1.0
    env:
    - name: LOG_LEVEL
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-config
          key: LOG_LEVEL
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-volume
      mountPath: /etc/config
  volumes:
  - name: config-volume
    configMap:
      name: app-config

data.title: ConfigMap vs env vars
data.text: ConfigMaps let you change configuration without rebuilding images. Mount them as volumes to pick up changes on the fly, or use environment variables for simpler key-value injection.

A **Secret** stores sensitive data such as passwords, OAuth tokens, and TLS certificates. Secrets are stored in base64-encoded form in etcd. They are **not encrypted by default** — you should use etcd encryption at rest and follow the principle of least privilege.

data.title: Creating a database Secret
data.content: Store database credentials as a Kubernetes Secret.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  username: YWRtaW4=
  password: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=

data.title: Decoding and creating secrets from CLI
data.content: Use the command line to create and inspect secrets.
data.code:
# Create a secret from literal values
kubectl create secret generic db-secret \
  --from-literal=username=admin \
  --from-literal=password=secret123

# Decode base64 to verify
echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=' | base64 --decode

cards.title: Secret
cards.description: Stores sensitive data, base64-encoded by default.

terms.definition: Stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs that Pods can consume.
Stores sensitive data like passwords and tokens in base64-encoded form.
An API object that manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to Services in a cluster.
A daemon (e.g., NGINX, Traefik) that enforces Ingress rules and routes traffic.

data.text: An **Ingress** is an API object that manages external access to services, typically HTTP/HTTPS. It acts as a reverse proxy and can do path-based or host-based routing. An **Ingress controller** (e.g., NGINX, Traefik) implements the rules — you need one installed in your cluster for Ingress to work.

data.caption: How ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Ingress fit into a cluster.
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[External User] --> B[Ingress Controller]
    B --> C[Ingress Rules]
    C --> D[Service A]
    C --> E[Service B]
    D --> F[Pods]
    E --> G[Pods]
    H[ConfigMap] --> F
    I[Secret] --> F

data.title: Ingress with path-based routing
data.content: Route traffic to different services based on the URL path.
data.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: app-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: myapp.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-service
            port:
              number: 8000
      - path: /web
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-service
            port:
              number: 80

data.text: Ingress can also terminate TLS. You create a Secret of type `tls` containing your certificate and private key, then reference it in the Ingress rule. This lets you serve HTTPS without a separate load balancer for each service.

data.title: Ingress with TLS
data.content: Configure HTTPS on an Ingress using a TLS secret.
data.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: secure-ingress
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - secure.myapp.com
    secretName: tls-secret
  rules:
  - host: secure.myapp.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-service
            port:
              number: 80

data.title: Ingress requires a controller
data.text: An Ingress resource alone does nothing — you must install an Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy, etc.) in your cluster for the rules to take effect.

data.title: Configure app secrets and routing
data.description: Apply ConfigMaps, Secrets, and an Ingress in a test cluster.
steps: Create a ConfigMap with non-secret configuration values.
Create a Secret with a username and password (base64-encoded).
Mount both into a Pod as environment variables.
Create an Ingress resource routing two paths to two services.
Verify the services are reachable through the Ingress.
data.expectedOutcome: Your app reads configuration from ConfigMaps/Secrets, and external traffic is routed by the Ingress.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration; Secrets store sensitive data (always base64-encoded).
Inject configuration via environment variables or volume mounts.
Ingress routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to Services based on host and path rules.
An Ingress controller must be installed for Ingress resources to function.
Use TLS secrets for HTTPS termination at the Ingress layer.
data.takeaway: Separate config from code, protect secrets, and route traffic with Ingress.
